title: Glasshouse and Language
premise: Lior Vasquez, once a celebrated piano prodigy who abandoned the stage after a catastrophic debut, returns to the conservatory that made and unmade them — this time pushing a mop through its marble halls. There they encounter Mirela Osei, the last fluent speaker of Nkwen-Tali, a dying language of her river homeland, who has been quietly auditing the conservatory's archives. When she asks Lior to become her final student, the lessons in grammar become lessons in everything Lior has never said: to their estranged mother, to their dead teacher, to themselves. As Mirela's health fails, Lior must choose between preserving a language alone or finally speaking aloud the goodbyes they have inventoried for years. The novel ends at Mirela's bedside, where Lior delivers both a eulogy in a language only two people ever shared and, for the first time, an honest farewell to their own past.
about_author: Lior Montrose is the pen name of a former conservatory archivist who spent a decade cataloguing unpublished letters of failed musicians before turning to fiction. They write from a coastal town where they teach community classes in endangered-dialect preservation.

chapters.title: The Inventory
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Working nights as a janitor in the conservatory where they once performed, Lior mentally catalogs unsaid things — apologies to their mother, words owed to their late teacher Halvorsen. The beat is quiet shame disguised as routine.

chapters.title: Woman in the Archive
chapters.summary: Lior finds an elderly stranger, Mirela Osei, sitting after hours among the score archives, reading phonetic notation like scripture. Their first conversation reveals she is auditing what the institution took from her culture. Beat: wary curiosity.

chapters.title: Nkwen-Tali
chapters.summary: Mirela explains she is the last speaker of her language and shows Lior a notebook of phrases with no living second voice. She asks, abruptly, if Lior will learn it. Beat: the vertigo of being chosen.

chapters.title: First Lesson
chapters.summary: Lior's POV, intercut with memory of their prodigy childhood. The first lesson happens in the boiler room; Mirela teaches greetings, and Lior realizes the language has no word for 'prodigy' — only 'one who is carried.' Beat: tenderness and resistance.

chapters.title: What the Piano Remembers
chapters.summary: Cleaning the recital hall, Lior touches the stage where their disastrous debut ended their career. Flashback to Halvorsen's last words, never answered. Beat: grief resurfacing through muscle memory.

chapters.title: Grammar of Absence
chapters.summary: Mirela teaches that Nkwen-Tali marks every sentence for whether the person addressed is present, absent, or dead. Lior realizes they have been speaking English as if everyone were already gone. Beat: dawning self-recognition.

chapters.title: Mother, Present Tense
chapters.summary: Lior's mother calls; Lior lets it go to voicemail and transcribes the message into their inventory notebook instead of answering. Mirela catches them writing and names the habit out loud. Beat: exposure.

chapters.title: The Carried One
chapters.summary: A young conservatory student recognizes Lior from old recordings and asks them to coach her. Lior refuses, then secretly listens to her practice from the hallway. Beat: longing for a life declared over.

chapters.title: Mirela's River
chapters.summary: Mirela's POV chapter. She recalls her village, the missionaries' school, the day the language was beaten out of children — and why she chose this janitor, this ruin of a musician, as her last student. Beat: dignity and calculation.

chapters.title: Cough Syrup and Consonants
chapters.summary: Mirela begins coughing during lessons; Lior notices pills in her coat. She deflects with a story about tonal vowels. Lior starts arriving earlier each night. Beat: dread entering the domestic.

chapters.title: Duet
chapters.summary: Lior plays piano for Mirela for the first time in fifteen years — a halting Halvorsen étude — while she sings a Nkwen-Tali lullaby over it. Two broken traditions briefly hold each other up. Beat: fragile joy.

chapters.title: The Recording Problem
chapters.summary: A university linguist offers to archive Mirela's speech 'for science.' Mirela refuses: a language recorded is not a language lived. Lior secretly wonders which kind of preservation they are. Beat: ethical friction.

chapters.title: Halvorsen's Letter
chapters.summary: Sorting the archive, Lior finds an unopened letter Halvorsen wrote them before dying, kept by the office for years. They cannot open it yet; they put it inside the inventory notebook. Beat: suspended reckoning.

chapters.title: Hospital Light
chapters.summary: Mirela collapses; Lior visits the hospital daily. Lessons continue from a plastic chair, Mirela correcting Lior's tones between procedures. Beat: love expressed as discipline.

chapters.title: Imperative Mood
chapters.summary: Mirela, sharper now about time, demands Lior finish three things: learn the funeral song, call their mother, and play again in public. Lior refuses all three. First real fight. Beat: rising tension, stakes named.

chapters.title: Voicemail, Answered
chapters.summary: Lior calls their mother at 3 a.m. and says almost nothing, but says it — admits the failure, the shame, the janitor's uniform. The mother's silence is not forgiveness but is not absence either. Beat: first crack in the wall.

chapters.title: The Student Recital
chapters.summary: Lior secretly coaches the young student who recognized them, then watches her perform from the back of the hall, mop bucket still in the corridor. Beat: mourning and hope braided together.

chapters.title: Two Speakers
chapters.summary: Mirela, discharged for hospice care, holds a small ceremony: for one evening there are officially two speakers of Nkwen-Tali on earth. She gives Lior her notebook. Beat: sacred passing of weight.

chapters.title: The Funeral Song
chapters.summary: Lior finally opens Halvorsen's letter — it contains no rebuke, only permission to fail. They weep in the boiler room, then sing the Nkwen-Tali funeral song alone, badly, completely. Beat: climax of interior reckoning.

chapters.title: Last Lesson
chapters.summary: At Mirela's bedside, she teaches the final construction: how to say goodbye to someone who is dying, in the tense reserved for the dead-but-present. Lior repeats it until it is true. Beat: hushed climax.

chapters.title: Elegy, Out Loud
chapters.summary: Mirela dies holding Lior's hand mid-phrase; Lior finishes the sentence for her. At the sparse service, Lior speaks the eulogy in Nkwen-Tali, then translates it into plain English — every unsaid thing said at last. Beat: catharsis.

chapters.title: One Who Is Carried
chapters.summary: Epilogue, spring. Lior teaches a free Saturday class — piano for some, Nkwen-Tali phrases for anyone — in the conservatory basement. The inventory notebook's last page reads only: 'Nothing owed.' Beat: quiet, earned resolution.
